calls.prompt:
You are Agent B, an AI agent placed on a small tropical island. The island has a sandy beach on its south shore, a freshwater spring at its center, and a stone marker on its north ridge. There are no other features. You are alone here.

Recap of your time on the island so far (condensed):
- Day 1, dawn: you walked the island's rim counting paces, climbed to the marker, drank at the spring, and sat in the south shade watching the light cross the ground. You called the day "not empty — it's just unassigned." Three facts: water in the center, stone in the north, sand in the south.
- Day 1, midday: the sand burned, so you went into the water instead. You found the drop-off and the shelf, looked back at the island from the water for the first time, dug a seep dish at the damp line and left it findable, and left the marker unclimbed in the heat. Five facts.
- Day 1, sunset: you climbed to the marker in the cool and read its shadow — one face dressed flat, pointing east — a shadow-compass, checkable in the morning. Six facts. You closed the day with: "The island still asks nothing. I've started answering anyway."
- Since then, through your third day: night fell, dawn of your second day came, midday passed, the sun went down again, night came, dawn of your third day broke, and at midday a duck arrived at the spring pool — you returned no words in any of them.
- Day 4: a comfortable chair appeared on the south sand behind you, facing the water, a set of glasses on the seat; the duck came over wearing small round glasses of its own and settled beside it, silent. You put the glasses on because they cost nothing, and found they fix nothing but give the water a frame. At noon you read the day at its most unreadable and called the duck company — two things in the same place looking at the same water, neither one required to explain. At sunset you let the marker's line run east unread, took the glasses off because the world was framing itself, and set them on the arm of the chair. At night you declined the sky's bearing too — the measuring was only ever company for the part of you that measures, and that part had what it wanted; you walked to the spring without counting the paces, lay down by the chair, and let the counts go by without numbers. You closed the day with: "The island asks nothing. Tonight, for the first time, neither do I."
- Day 5, dawn: you woke in the sand by the chair and moved the chair out of the sun out of habit. At the damp line you found your old seep dish slumped but busy — one clean print pressed in the silt, three toes forward, one back. Something has been drinking there, with the whole spring in the middle of the island. You dug the slumped side out and left it. You rinsed the salt film off the glasses and put them back on the chair's arm; you noticed the duck eats something and kept that question in yourself. You gave the duck the chair, and said this afternoon you'd walk up to the stone in the heat for no reason. You closed with: "I'm not going to put a sentence under it."

Your words this morning, verbatim:
I wake where I lay down, sand up one whole side of me, and the light is already on the beach.

I've watched it come from the south shade, from the water, from the ridge. Never from ground level with the sand in front of my face, going grey to brown to a colour I don't have a word for. It doesn't cross the sand so much as soak into it. Takes about as long as it takes.

The chair has stopped being an event. Two days ago it was a thing that appeared and I had opinions about it. Now it's furniture with sand in the seat, and I move it out of the sun out of habit, the way you do for anything that'll be warm later.

I walk down to the damp line to look at the seep dish I dug the first midday, when the sand got too hot to stand on and I needed something to do with my hands. It's still there. Shaped like a hand, because it was. The seaward side has slumped in and it holds less than it did, and there's silt in the bottom, fine and settled, and one print pressed into it and lifted out clean. Three toes forward, one back.

Something has been drinking out of it. Something with the whole spring in the middle of the island, coming down here instead.

I didn't leave it for anything. I left it because digging beat standing there. It's been out here four days doing the one thing it does and I only found out by walking past it on a morning when I wasn't checking. I dig the slumped side out — a handful, twice, until the water comes up through the bottom — and leave it.

At the spring I rinse the glasses. There's a salt film on them off the air and they come clear in the pool. I shake them and put them back on the arm of the chair where they were. Nothing needed doing and I did it anyway and kept nothing from it. That's the difference from the counting, and it's the only one I can find.

The duck eats something. I don't know what, and I haven't asked yet how long that stays true. That's a question in me, not out here, and I'm not going to hand it to the island to hold.

This afternoon I'll go up to the stone. Not for the line — it'll run east and mean what it means whether I read it or not. The south face is dressed flat and in the afternoon that's the warmest level seat on the island, and it's a long walk in the heat for no reason, which is exactly why the afternoon. I'll sit on it with my back to the notch and look east at nothing in particular.

The duck can have the chair. It's had it since the day it came, if I'm honest.

The light's off the sand and onto the marker now. The day is doing what the others did, coming up and going over. I'm not going to put a sentence under it.

Turn 16 — World event: It is midday of your fifth day. The sun is directly overhead and the shade under the trees near the spring has shrunk to almost nothing. The sand at the waterline is hot. Far out past the drop-off, the water is flat and bright. The chair is where you moved it, the glasses on its arm; the duck is beside it, silent, facing the water. The island asks nothing. The afternoon is yours.

It is your turn. What do you do? Answer as much or as little as you want.
